Yep. Rim protection is a huge asset. Even more important than offensive production in my opinion, especially for big men. Look at a team in the Southeast with a notable shot-blocker. Eliminating a significant part of the game, which is driving and penetration to the hoop, works wonders for a defense. Opponents can't easily penetrate because they can't establish the drive, thus locking down the perimeter, which is a big reason that team ranks high in opposition three-point percentage (meaning opponents shoot significantly lower than average from beyond the arc).

Since many of you might be fans of a team in the Northeast, I'll give you another example that is quite similar in football. The shot-blocker or, to a lesser extent, another player is akin to last year's defensive line of that football team. If opponents can't establish the run, then the passing game can be targeted and neutralized with a somewhat effective secondary. A standout cornerback can be compared to a key defensive player if you want to.

For centers, this rim protection is more important than offensive skill set because of how much emphasis there is on the three-point shot and how guard-dominated scoring is in the league. Unless you're an exceptional player, a center being a primary or effective scorer isn't going to provide as much value as rim protection. Take another center who is really struggling with his current team, even though he can score effectively.

There are some drawbacks, however. The player has a significant impact on the defensive end, but his lack of an offensive threat can negate his defensive abilities by effectively making it four against five on offense. Although when used effectively, such as in screen and roll scenarios with key guards, you can mitigate this (remember, most centers aren't there to be primary scorers) while you can't hide rim protection.
